source: Murphy et al. (2008) Debugging: the good, the bad, and the quirky (Crossref record only)
finding: Gap 1 attempt. Crossref lists the record under the short title Debugging, with no abstract. The ACM PDF returned HTTP 403. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate limited and the WebSearch budget was used up. The full text could not be read.
numbers: Crossref: 42 citations, 13 references. No sample size or strategy counts obtained.
limits: Gap 1 stays open. Do not quote Murphy numbers from memory.
agent_relevance: Needs a library copy before any Murphy figure is used in the schema.

source: Fitzgerald et al. (2008) Debugging: finding, fixing and flailing (Crossref record only)
finding: Gap 1 attempt. Crossref has the title and 147 citations but no abstract. The Taylor and Francis PDF returned HTTP 403. Only the second-hand claim from Kurniawan et al. (line a12) is available: once students locate a bug they usually fix it.
numbers: Crossref: 147 citations, 14 references. No sample or rates obtained.
limits: Gap 1 stays open for Fitzgerald.
agent_relevance: Finding the bug, not fixing it, is the hard step for novices, but this is second-hand.

source: Qian & Lehman (2017) Students' misconceptions and other difficulties in introductory programming: a literature review (Crossref abstract)
finding: Gap 9 attempt. The Crossref abstract was read. The review sorts novice difficulties into syntactic, conceptual and strategic knowledge. Causes named: unfamiliar syntax, natural language, maths background, inaccurate mental models, lack of strategies, programming environments, teacher knowledge. Many difficulties trace back to prior knowledge. It asks for a move from cataloguing misconceptions to conceptual change theory.
numbers: Crossref: 127 references, 466 citations. The abstract holds no counts for any single misconception.
quote: many sources of students' difficulties have connections with students' prior knowledge
limits: Abstract only. The ACM PDF was 403. No per-misconception counts, so a seeded misconception test set cannot yet be built from it.
agent_relevance: Use the three-way split (syntax, concept, strategy) to stratify seeded bugs. Counts still needed.

source: McCauley et al. (2008) review, handout extracts (re-opened)
finding: Gap 9 attempt. The open handout was fetched again and run through pdftotext. It gave only about 2 KB of text, with no counts, percentages or sample sizes, and nothing on Murphy or Fitzgerald results.
numbers: No numbers extractable.
limits: Extract only. Earlier lines b01 and b02 already hold what is usable.
agent_relevance: None new. Top-misconception counts for McCauley remain unknown.

source: Xu et al. (2025) Exploring the Potential and Limitations of LLMs for Novice Program Fault Localization
finding: Thirteen LLMs (six closed, seven open) localise faults in 503 novice-level programs per dataset (Codeflaws in C, Condefects in Java, BugT in C++; BugT was built from a closed university judge to avoid leakage). Each run was repeated 5 times. Reasoning models beat older chat models, and LLMs beat spectrum and mutation methods. Top-1 counts out of 503 for OpenAI o3: Codeflaws 99, Condefects 312, BugT 289. GPT-4o: 101, 213, 177. GPT-3.5-Turbo: 100, 148, 133. DeepSeekR1 on BugT: 248. GPT-4o matched or beat o3 on Top-1 on Codeflaws.
numbers: o3 Top-1 rate: 19.7% Codeflaws, 62.0% Condefects, 57.5% BugT (counts over 503). Top-5 for o3: 291, 409, 449.
limits: Codeflaws is public and may be in training data. Some table cells are garbled in the PDF text, so only clean rows are quoted.
agent_relevance: Gives a 2025 baseline for novice bug localisation to test any scaffold against. Large model gaps mean a scaffold must be tested per model class.

source: Xu et al. (2025) prompt ablation (same paper, RQ3)
finding: Five prompt parts were removed one at a time: novice background, chain of thought, stated code intent, justification, ranking. Run on 50 programs per dataset for o3, DeepSeekR1 and GPT-4. For o3 and DeepSeekR1, removing parts barely mattered and sometimes performance rose. For GPT-4 every removal hurt, and dropping the novice description hurt most: Top-1 fell by 7 (77.77%) on Condefects, 3 (42.8%) on Codeflaws, 5 (38.36%) on BugT.
numbers: 50 programs per dataset; Top-1 drops of 7, 3 and 5 programs for GPT-4 without the novice description.
limits: Tiny samples. The novice description is role context, not a staged hypothesis-test process. No equal-token control.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 2: explicit prompt structure helps a non-reasoning model but not reasoning models. A staged process is likely redundant for strong reasoners and useful for weaker ones. Hypothesis, test, localise staging itself was not tested.

source: Xu et al. (2025) difficulty, explanation ratings and cost (same paper, RQ4, RQ5, Table 5)
finding: Accuracy falls as problems get harder. o3 Top-1 per difficulty bucket on Condefects: 71 (hardest) to 91 (easiest); on Codeflaws 44 to 64. Ten novice participants rated explanations; one-year-experience raters rated them consistently high, three-year raters discriminated more. Cost per program: o3 $0.0152 and 52.4 s, GPT-4o $0.0092 and 15.3 s, o1-preview $0.4859 and 96.4 s, GPT-3.5-Turbo $0.0034 and 7.3 s. The authors report over-reasoning in some models.
numbers: 10 raters; costs per program as listed.
limits: Ten raters. Rating is perceived usefulness, not learning.
agent_relevance: Difficulty-dependent accuracy gives a natural stratum for seeded bugs. Cost figures help set equal-token comparisons.

source: Kopytskyi et al. (2026) SocraticRepair: planning-guided Socratic tutoring
finding: A Qwen2.5-Coder-7B model fine-tuned on 1,213 synthetic dialogues (419 programming cases, 8,493 tutor turns) is compared with GPT-4o on 53 held-out cases, 159 dialogues per tutor, with simulated students. Premature answer disclosure: 1.88% of turns (24 of 1,276) versus 7.43% (59 of 794); dialogue level 12.6% (20 of 159) versus 33.3% (53 of 159). Mean rounds 8.04 versus 4.99. Completed dialogues 93.1% versus 95.6%.
numbers: 159 dialogues per tutor; 53 cases.
limits: Student, tutor and judges are all LLMs. Human check on only 40 turns. A fine-tuned 7B model, not a prompt scaffold.
agent_relevance: A plan-then-ask structure cuts early answer reveal. Relevant to a rule of not stating a fix before a hypothesis is checked.

source: Kopytskyi et al. (2026) SocraticRepair quality scores and plan validity (same paper)
finding: On 158 matched dialogues (0 to 2 scale, Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon): question quality 1.626 vs 1.446 (p<.001) and stepwise scaffolding 1.876 vs 1.789 (p=.006) favour SocraticRepair; technical correctness 1.789 vs 1.860 (p=.002) and adaptive feedback 1.792 vs 1.843 (p=.036) favour GPT-4o; relevance and progression did not differ. The learned planner made a technically valid plan in only 11 of 53 cases (41 of 52 plans had a technical error), while GPT-4o plus a verifier produced 53 of 53 valid plans.
numbers: Human versus judge agreement (Cohen kappa) 0.66 to 0.81 on 40 turns.
limits: Simulated students. The verified-plan condition was used for the score table.
agent_relevance: Planning without a correctness check is fragile. An independent verifier for the plan fixed it. Supports the verify-before-assert guardrail and partly speaks to gap 4.

source: Sankaranarayanan (2026) Mitigating Epistemic Debt in AI-Scaffolded Novice Programming
finding: Randomised between-subjects study, N=78 (26 per group), Claude 3.5 Sonnet in a code editor. Phase 1: build an app. Phase 2 with AI revoked: fix an injected race-condition bug. Repair success: manual 18 of 26 (69.2%), unrestricted AI 6 of 26 (23.1%), scaffolded AI with a teach-back Explanation Gate 16 of 26 (61.5%); chi-square(2)=13.8, p=.001. Phase 1 utility: manual 65.2%, unrestricted 92.4%, scaffolded 89.1%.
numbers: N=78; chi-square(2)=13.8, p=.001; utility ANOVA F(2,75)=48.2, eta-squared=0.56.
limits: Single 90-minute session on one day, so not long-term. Online recruits. Phase 2 has one bug. Hawthorne effect acknowledged. Single author.
agent_relevance: Strong current-tool evidence that unrestricted help leaves novices worse at debugging without it, and that a forced explanation step removes most of the loss. Gap 6 only partly closed: no delayed retention.

source: Sankaranarayanan (2026) Explanation Gate cost and interaction stances (same paper)
finding: The gate cost time. The manual group hit the 90-minute cap with 42% of requirements met; both AI groups reached 100%. Gate time median 14.2 minutes; the scaffolded group was slower than the unrestricted group (p<.001, d=1.52). In the unrestricted group, the 6 who fixed the bug asked 4.2 explanatory prompts per session versus 0.4 for those who failed (t(24)=5.1, d=2.37). 72% of gated users first called the gate annoying; 64% of those who fixed the bug said it told them where to look.
numbers: Gate median 14.2 min; d=1.52; d=2.37; 72% and 64%.
limits: Some table cells are garbled in the PDF text, so only the stated medians and effect sizes are used. The stance analysis is a post-hoc look at 6 successes.
agent_relevance: The consultant stance (ask why) predicts later repair skill. For an agent the analogue is explaining its own fix. The gate was forced, not user-triggered, so it does not replicate the b17 timing result.

source: Eastwood et al. (2026) Guardrails or Roadblocks? Socratic vs Direct AI teaching assistants
finding: Randomised trial, N=132 intro students, four AI TAs: Socratic or Direct, with or without full context of the problem and code. Socratic plus full context was rated worst for support in finishing the task. Full comprehension of the debugging fix: Direct+Full 67%, Direct+No context 61%, Socratic+No context 50%, Socratic+Full 48% (overall 57% full, 30% partial, 11% minimal among 128 responses). Use of another LLM: 23% (7 of 30) in Socratic+Full versus 9 to 15% elsewhere (15% overall).
numbers: N=132; perceived comprehension support chi-square(3)=4.79, p=.188; queries per problem 11.1 (Socratic no context) vs 5.1, 4.1, 4.7; message length chi-square(3)=29.96, p<.001.
limits: Comprehension and external-LLM differences were not statistically significant. One session, three tasks. Open-ended recall, hand coded.
agent_relevance: Contradicts the idea that Socratic-first always helps: no significant learning gain, lower satisfaction, drift to other tools. A question-first mode needs a test on task success, not only style.

source: Mihaylova et al. (2026) Effects of Structured LLM-Generated Feedback on Programming Assignment Performance
finding: Online course data, 111 novice and 38 advanced students. Three LLM feedback types (general, single-issue, diagnostic) versus compiler messages only. All were linked to faster time to success; log-time coefficients: single-issue -0.214, diagnostic -0.194, general -0.122. Attempts coefficients: diagnostic -0.200, general -0.175, single-issue -0.090 (94% HDI exclude 0). Feedback looked more helpful for advanced than novice students, but with no strong interaction.
numbers: 111 novice plus 38 advanced students; Bayesian mixed models.
limits: Observational course data, not a randomised learning test. Effects on later skill were not measured. Cases of wrong-issue feedback were noted.
agent_relevance: Less guided, more focused feedback worked best for speed. Evidence that fewer, targeted issues beat verbose diagnosis, in line with the false-issue worry.

source: Andleeb et al. (2025) ChatGPT in Introductory Programming: Counterbalanced Evaluation
finding: Quasi-experimental crossover in a CS1 course, two C assignments, ChatGPT or not. Lab task completion time: assignment 1 GPT 494.9 s versus 2385.3 s without; assignment 2 868.0 s versus 1934.3 s without (p=.0002 and p=.0011). Code quality rubric higher with ChatGPT. Conceptual post-survey: assignment 1 total not different (U=153.5, p=.32); assignment 2 total U=77.0, p=.0457, but no single question significant. Abstract reports mixed concept gains (lower for functions, higher for structures).
numbers: Times in seconds as listed; U and p as listed.
limits: Students self-selected into groups by registration. Single course. The post-survey is a short quiz taken straight after the task.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as Kazemitabaar: big speed and quality gains while using the tool, unclear learning. No delayed retention.

source: Santos & Becker (2024) Not the Silver Bullet: LLM-enhanced error messages are ineffective in practice
finding: Within-subjects, N=106 intro students fixing six buggy C programs, each with a compiler message, an expert handwritten message or a GPT-4 explanation. GPT-4 messages gave a faster time to fix than compiler messages in only 1 of 6 tasks. Handwritten explanations beat both. Students fixed 98% of exercises overall.
numbers: N=106; 6 tasks; 1 of 6 tasks significant for GPT-4; 98% fixed overall.
limits: GPT-4 of 2024; one language; ceiling on fix rate.
agent_relevance: Fluent explanation does not equal faster repair. Matches K02. A scaffold must be judged on repair, not on how good the text reads.

source: Moraru et al. (2026) Skill-targeted LLM error messages, crowd study
finding: N=103 crowd workers, split by a proficiency test into 38 novices and 65 experts, fixing Python snippets with a standard, a pragmatic or a contingent (scaffolded) LLM message. Subjective ratings rose for LLM messages, but gains in objective fix rate, attempts and time were not significant. Fix rate for novices: standard 46%, pragmatic 54%, contingent 42%; experts: 68%, 82%, 90%. Per-snippet fix rates ranged from 53% to 84%.
numbers: N=103; novice n=38, expert n=65.
limits: Small cells; crowd workers, not students; snippet effects vary widely. The paper itself draws no firm conclusion on style effects.
agent_relevance: Second independent source that nicer explanations are not better debugging. Scaffolded style helped experts more than novices, a warning against assuming scaffolds help weak users.

source: MacNeil et al. (2024) Decoding Logic Errors: students versus LLMs
finding: 964 students, GPT-3 and GPT-4 looked for logic bugs in three C code examples (with variants). Overall correct rate: GPT-3 85.3%, GPT-4 85.0%, students 49.1%. On faulty code GPT-3 reached 87.3%. GPT-4 found 1.70 more bugs than students (mixed model, p<0.001). Models raised false bugs in correct code (for example 6 for GPT-4 in one correct example). GPT-4 reports averaged 129 words versus 38.9 for students.
numbers: N=964 students; rates as listed.
limits: GPT-3 and GPT-4 of 2023 and short single-function code, so the false-issue rate is not comparable to the Hellas help-request set.
agent_relevance: Shows false positives on correct code persist in GPT-4 on this task. Gap 3 is only indirectly informed: no 2025 to 2026 model was re-run on the Hellas set.

source: Al-Hossami et al. (2023) Can Language Models Employ the Socratic Method? Experiments with code debugging
finding: Benchmark of 38 problems and 151 Socratic dialogues. Manual precision, recall and F1 of instructor utterances: GPT-3.5 22.8, 21.7, 22.2; with chain of thought 18.6, 5.5, 8.5. GPT-4 42.5, 42.7, 42.6; with chain of thought 38.2, 57.5, 45.9. Fine-tuned Flan-T5 did poorly on the held-out set.
numbers: Manual F1 as listed; 149 utterances over 43 turns in 11 dialogues were hand scored.
limits: Small manual sample. Chain of thought here is utterance planning, not computing a counterexample.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: step-by-step reasoning helped the bigger model (F1 +3.3) and hurt the smaller (F1 -13.7). That is the opposite of the claim that reasoning helps small models more.

source: Lee et al. (2024) Improving LLM classification of logical errors by integrating error relationships into prompts
finding: Adding descriptions of logical-error types and their relations to chain and tree of thought prompts raised GPT-3.5-turbo classification accuracy from 35% (30 of 86) to 56% (48 of 86), a 21 point rise. Some types such as Conceptual stayed low (0 of 6 rising to 2 of 6).
numbers: 86 programs; accuracy 35% to 56%.
limits: Small set; GPT-3.5; classification of a seeded error type, not repair.
agent_relevance: A taxonomy of bug types in the prompt may help a weaker model name the error. Related to the misconception diagnosis step (gap 5), but it is bug types, not wrong beliefs.

source: Van Mullem et al. (2026) Evaluating LLMs for Answering Student Questions in Introductory Programming
finding: 170 real CS1 student questions with expert answers; a validated LLM judge (Pearson r=0.8185, Spearman 0.7982, 91.66% within one point). Educator answers scored a mean 2.925 of 5. Almost all current models beat that; Gemini 3 flash scored 3.335, with 52.35% of answers at 4 or higher and 82.35% at 3 or higher; Gemini 2.0 Flash had 29.4% at 4 or higher. Only GPT 5 mini did not exceed the human baseline. Turning off thinking in Claude Opus 4.5 cut cost 47.41% and score 6.03%.
numbers: 170 questions; 134 with a valid educator answer.
limits: Question answering, not bug diagnosis; the judge is an LLM; the paper still advises a teacher in the loop against hallucination.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partial: current models now beat typical educators on general student questions. The 40% false-issue rate on help requests with code was not re-measured.
